newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices fall as low fuel stock fears ease.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices fall as low fuel stock fears ease.

text.p: World oil prices eased on Tuesday as traders' concern about a possible shortage of winter heating oil in Europe subsided on signs that supplies in the European market were increasing.
A report released on Tuesday showed a healthy build in October of distillate stocks, including heating oil, held in the European Union.

Compounding Tuesday's bearish tone was news that the key Rotterdam market is about to receive extra supplies following the expiration of the November gas oil (heating oil) futures contract on London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE).
The bearish tone spilled over into crude oil. World benchmark Brent futures on the IPE ended 21 cents below Monday's close at $22.80.
The entire energy complex has been supported for several weeks on traders' concerns that low heating oil inventories on both sides of the Atlantic would fail to meet peak winter demand.

But European and U.S. refineries have been producing flat-out to replenish product stocks, which has taken some of the bite out of a blistering oil price rally which in mid-October sent crude to its highest levels since the end of the 1991 Gulf War.

Currently, oil prices are around $2 off their mid-October peak but traders say it is too early in the season to sell the market aggressively in case there is a repeat of last winter's frigid temperatures.
A record 865,100 tonnes of gas oil delivered against the expired IPE contract, equivalent to one third of the storage capacity in the key Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp (ARA) refining region.
"The reaction is that there is lots of supply around," said Charles Gray of Prudential-Bache futures brokers in London.
Most of the heating oil is earmarked for one large trading house which is expected to ship its share to the Far East.
"Most of it won't hang around in ARA for long, but it's still putting the pressure on," Gray said.

Data released on Tuesday by the Euroilstock Foundation showed that middle distillate stocks in the European Union, excluding Sweden, rose by 6.60 million barrels (880,000 tonnes) or 2.3 percent in October, trimming the deficit from year-ago levels to 21.65 million barrels (2.88 million tonnes), or 6.9 percent.

Traders are now waiting to see if weekly stock data from the American Petroleum Institute (API), to be released after the close of trading on Tuesday, will show the rebuilding trend continuing in the United States.
"The market is in pre-API mode," Gray said. "We're expecting a build in heating oil, but that should be balanced by a draw on gasoline stocks."
